text:
At the laundrette, a blue sheet makes one last turn behind the round glass. It rises, folds over itself, and slides to the bottom of the drum.

The machine stops. A loose corner slips an inch farther and stays there.

Beside it, an older woman pairs two thick socks, smoothing each heel with her thumb. She has brought a basket lined with a towel. The clean clothes go into it without being pressed flat, soft hills of cotton, still holding a little of the machine's warmth.

Her coat is on the chair. For a while she leaves it there.

text:
Beneath the greenhouse bench
a terracotta saucer holds
three fallen petals.

A bead of water hangs
from the watering can's bent spout.
It grows heavy,
drops,
and makes a dark spot in the dust.

Along the glass,
a bean tendril has found the string.
Its small curl closes there,
so gradually that the change
belongs to another day.

The gardener's hat rests on a peg.
In the turned-up brim,
a dry leaf has come to rest.

text:
The bookshop owner found a pressed fern between the pages of an atlas. Its stalk had made a pale line down the fold, and the smaller leaves were almost transparent.

She carried the book to the deep window seat. A bus went by, making the pane tremble softly in its frame. The fern did not move.

After a while she laid a clean sheet of paper beneath it and closed the atlas only halfway. There was room on the cushion for the book and for her. She sat there until the glass stopped feeling cool against her shoulder.

In the small music room, the piano lid is raised a hand's breadth. A single low note has nearly finished sounding.

The felt inside takes back the last of it. A pedal returns slowly beneath the bench, with a faint wooden knock.

On the open score, a pencil lies across two empty bars. Its varnish is worn away where a hand has held it for years. Through the doorway comes the soft brush of a broom along the corridor, advancing a little, pausing, advancing again.

The room keeps the shape of the note after the sound is gone.

text:
The woollen blanket hangs over the washing line,
its two sides almost touching the grass.

Wind lifts one corner.
The whole broad weight of it follows,
then lowers,
and the line gives a small creak at the post.

Along the hem, a patch of blue cloth
has faded to the same grey as the wool.
The stitches hold it as they always have.

A beetle crosses the wooden peg,
feels for the other side,
and disappears beneath the spring.

The blanket moves once more.
The grass bends under its passing edge.

text:
On the bakery rack, the round loaves are cooling. Every so often one gives a fine crackle, too small a sound to tell which loaf made it.

Flour has settled in the grain of the long table. A baker brushes some into her palm and tips it back into the tin. Then she sits on the low stool by the doorway, her apron folded loosely across her knees.

The bread gives up its heat a little at a time. By the bottom shelf, the air smells faintly of toasted seed. A crumb falls through the rack and lands beside her shoe.
